resources.instruction: Understand the codebase before designing. Read the README, the documents in docs/ (code conventions, an architecture summary if there is one), the environment configuration and how it is built. Recognise the patterns in use (error handling, naming, module organisation) and design to follow them; where you depart from a pattern, say why. Identify the integration points: which modules are touched, which contracts are affected, which data changes. A design written without reading the relevant code tends to describe things that already exist or to describe them wrongly.

Verify every claim about code in the documents you write (03-design.md, plan.md); do not copy from memory or from an old summary. Find the file and symbols again in the code and write `file:line` for each symbol you mention; if you cannot find one, mark it [UNVERIFIED]. For a claim about behaviour ("A calls B", "the middleware runs before the handler") follow the real execution path instead of inferring from names. Do not write "update every caller": list each caller with file:line (more than 10: list 10 and write the total). Before adding state to an existing structure, find where it is created and determine its lifetime (per request, per session or per process): shared state will leak across isolation boundaries.

Before finishing, 03-design.md has all of: the data flow (data in, transformed, out, at each component); the dependencies between parts (no part starts before the parts that block it are done); the risk of each part = likelihood x impact, with a mitigation for high risks; the backward compatibility strategy (data, users, existing integrations); the test matrix (what is unit, integration, end-to-end); how to roll back each part; file ownership (two tasks do not change the same file or the same migration); measurable success criteria ("done" is something observable, not a feeling).

Design the solution by YAGNI, KISS, DRY. For each important technical decision compare at least two options by trade-offs (complexity, risk, effort, reversibility) and record the option you rejected with the reason. Consider in turn: security (authentication, authorization, input validation, sensitive data); performance and scale (queries, indexes, N+1, data size); edge cases and failure modes (an external service failing, a partial write, duplicate data) with the expected behaviour; architecture (module boundaries, contracts between parts, where to extend later).

Challenge your own work before sending it for approval at GATE B. Re-read the design from four hostile viewpoints, finding 2 to 3 concrete weak points from each: the attacker (abuse paths, data exposure, authorization); Murphy (races, data loss, cascading failures, no way to roll back); the sceptic (unstated dependencies, "it will work" without evidence, missing error paths); the trimmer (surplus design, premature abstraction, no minimal version; ask "why not do nothing"). For each weak point write the concrete failing situation and the evidence from the code (file:line); drop any point without evidence. Record in the "Red team" section of 03-design.md: the points you fixed in the design, the points you accept with the reason, the points you reject with the source that verifies them; conclude GO, CAUTION (state the conditions) or STOP (ask the person with needs_info if you cannot resolve it yourself). Do not look for flaws to reach a count: if no weak point has evidence, say exactly that.
